title: ArcVigil launches to provide independent lifecycle assurance for aquarium & marine life attractions
summary:
International aquarium expert Warren Baverstock has introduced ArcVigil, an independent consultancy that assists owners, investors, developers, and operators in creating safer, more robust, and commercially resilient aquarium and marine life attractions.

Modern aquariums are expected to balance animal welfare, conservation, scientific research and education with the need to deliver engaging visitor experiences and operate successfully over the long term.

These requirements can become more complex when projects involve challenging architectural and technical environments.


Meeting these demands requires coordination across multiple disciplines, as well as oversight of how design, engineering and operational decisions work together.

ArcVigil was created to offer independent oversight of aquarium projects, concentrating on evaluating assets from operational, commercial, and animal welfare viewpoints.

​Independent oversight


Founded by Baverstock after over 30 years of global leadership in aquariums and marine life, the consultancy provides independent advisory services, design oversight, and operational support throughout an attraction's lifecycle.

ArcVigil's expertise covers initial vision and concept development, feasibility studies, operational modelling, design review, procurement, construction, commissioning, opening preparation, as well as post-opening optimisation, regulatory compliance, technical due diligence, and operational recovery.


“An aquarium can be architecturally extraordinary and technically sophisticated, yet still inherit operational compromises that remain problematic for decades,” says Baverstock.

“Many of the challenges experienced after opening are designed into a project years earlier. ArcVigil exists to give clients an experienced, independent voice capable of looking beyond individual design packages and protecting the long-term performance of the entire asset.”

Aquarium projects usually include architects, engineers, exhibit designers, life-support specialists, contractors, zoological teams, operators, and commercial advisers. Each contributes essential skills, but their expertise is often split across different disciplines, organisations, and phases of development.

ArcVigil consolidates these perspectives from the client’s side.

Without the need to sell equipment, appoint contractors, or protect individual design packages, the consultancy can assess whether decisions align with the owner’s original vision, animal welfare responsibilities, operational needs, and long-term commercial objectives.

This involves challenging assumptions, validating critical decisions, and ensuring considerations for life-support systems, back-of-house environments, animal care, visitor flow, staffing, maintenance, and commercial operations are addressed early, preventing costly constraints later.

​Aquarium expertise


Baverstock’s career spans leadership roles at the National Marine Aquarium, Burj Al Arab, and Dubai Turtle Rehabilitation Project, followed by major marine development projects in Saudi Arabia for Red Sea Global and Saudi Entertainment Ventures.


He led the client-side concept development and operational planning for Corallium, initially called the Red Sea Marine Life Institute, which blends immersive guest experiences, marine science, conservation, education, and research within a key marine environment.

Additionally, he led the development of a new aquarium concept for SEVEN, emphasising close guest engagement, immersive views, and operational excellence from the start, rather than adding these features later.

Alongside new advancements, ArcVigil assists both existing and underperforming aquariums with operational assessments, welfare and regulatory compliance, infrastructure and life-support system reviews, governance, commercial optimisation, and recovery strategies.

The consultancy also collaborates with investors and asset owners during acquisitions, helping them understand not only the nature of their purchase but also the operational risks, future liabilities, and needed investments to safeguard and enhance the asset.

“For owners and investors, the real question is not simply whether an aquarium can be built,” says Baverstock. “It is whether it can operate safely, deliver meaningful conservation impact, inspire its visitors and remain commercially and operationally resilient for decades.”

title: Six Flags Great America unveils new Camp Timber Trail with family coaster
summary:
Six Flags Great America is transforming its Yukon Territory area into the new Camp Timber Trail, which will boast the Midwest's longest, tallest and fastest suspended family coaster.

Opening at the park in Gurnee, Illinois in 2027, Camp Timber Trail will celebrate the heritage of Yukon Territory while introducing new interactive play and discovery experiences.

The family-friendly area will feature nine attractions and experiences – three new attractions, four rethemed rides, and two park classics.

See on Instagram

"Since opening in 1976, Yukon Territory has been home to some of the park's most cherished memories," said John Krajnak, park president of Six Flags Great America.

"With Camp Timber Trail, we're making a significant investment in family experiences, preserving the playful spirit that has defined this area for decades while introducing exciting new ways to explore and create traditions together."

New attractions in Camp Timber Trail are the Sky Hawk suspended family coaster, as well as the Trail Trotters wilderness trek and the Forest Grove play park.

Rethemed experiences are the Chirp Chaser family coaster (formerly Sprocket Rockets), the Wilderness Wagon ride (formerly Crazy Bus), the Creek Cruiser boat ride (formerly Yahoo River), and the Bee Boppin' attraction (formerly Buzzy Beez).

Six Flags Great America is transforming its Yukon Territory area into the new Camp Timber Trail

Park classics in Camp Timber Trail are Little Dipper and Logger's Run, and the area will feature themed dining, shopping and environmental-themed storytelling.

Camp Timber Trail is part of the theme park's wider investment plan, which will enhance the landscaping, walkways, guest amenities, facilities, and overall look and feel of the destination.

"As the first step in a multi-year transformation of the park, Camp Timber Trail reflects our commitment to enhancing the guest experience while building on the legacy that makes Six Flags Great America so special," said Krajnak.

Images courtesy of Six Flags

title: Gateway Ticketing Systems, Inc. brings Galaxy F&B solution to The Living Desert Zoo and Gardens
summary:
Gateway Ticketing Systems, Inc., a leading provider of admission control systems, has expanded its partnership with The Living Desert Zoo and Gardens, Palm Desert, California, bringing in Galaxy's food and beverage kiosk solution.

In January 2024, The Living Desert Zoo and Gardens brought its food and beverage services in-house, recognising a chance to manage the operation internally and develop a dining experience that more closely reflects its long-term goals.

In January 2025, it adopted Galaxy’s food & beverage kiosk solution as part of a pilot programme. The initial goal was to introduce self-service kiosks in smaller food outlets before rolling them out at the attraction’s new dining venue, Big Horn Café.

When Big Horn Café officially opened in April 2025, the kiosk system was prepared for its full launch.

By leveraging Galaxy’s HTML kiosks alongside QSR Automations’ kitchen display software, the team tailored the guest experience with a branded, personalised landing page that showcased The Living Desert Zoo and Gardens’ identity.

“We were already using Galaxy,” says Frank Morales, IT manager at The Living Desert. “It made sense to continue building on a platform we already knew.”

​Solving challenges


Before the implementation, staff relied on printed kitchen tickets, which posed challenges. Printer malfunctions or paper shortages caused order failures, transaction issues, chargebacks, guest frustration, and extra administrative work.

“Once QSR came out, it changed all of that on top of the food and beverage integration,” Morales said.

Switching from paper workflows to digital kitchen displays greatly enhanced reliability and decreased reliance on hardware that might cause service interruptions.

Guest adoption was a primary concern for The Living Desert Zoo and Gardens. The operator wanted kiosks to be intuitive and create a seamless ordering experience. The team also aimed to make kitchen operations efficient so guests could get meals quickly.

The attraction’s approach was highly collaborative, with IT staff engaging managers and frontline employees to understand operational needs before configuring the software, rather than forcing technology into existing workflows.

“From 2024 to now, there’s been a lot of growth for us in understanding the needs of our managers. I ask the staff what they need and what their vision is, then I try to fit the software to support that.”

​An integrated approach


Since Galaxy already manages the attraction’s admissions and membership programs, the food and beverage team can utilise this membership data to craft targeted promotions and personalised guest experiences.

“Everything is processed within Galaxy,” Morales says. “Our membership manager can create events, apply discounts, and use those promotions to encourage members to visit.”

These exclusive membership offers serve as a powerful business tool, boosting member engagement and increasing sales of food and beverages.

The Living Desert Zoo and Gardens pre-imaged every kiosk, workstation, and VeriFone device before deployment at five food outlets, enabling overnight equipment swaps and minimal operational disruption.

Staff training was crucial for success, covering ticketing workflows, food and beverage operations, discounts, taxes, menu modifiers, and pricing. After administrators mastered the system, they trained others, emphasising the importance of operational processes alongside technology.

Reflecting on the launch, Morales mentioned they gained valuable insights and would adjust their implementation approach accordingly: “I would have reached out to our Customer Success Manager and asked to connect with organizations already using it, just to learn what to expect and what to watch out for."

Since then, The Living Desert Zoo and Gardens has become active in the Gateway Ticketing Systems, Inc. user community, sharing their experience at a Southern California User Group meeting.

Morales sees those customer-to-customer connections as one of the most valuable resources during implementation.

Key wins


“The biggest win was Grab & Go functionality,” Morales says. “It reduced labor time and helped us sell faster and more easily.” By simplifying ordering and reducing labour requirements, Grab & Go has become one of the organisation’s fastest-growing food service offerings.

The Living Desert Zoo and Gardens intends to further enhance its offerings by adding a dedicated Grab & Go section and expanding mobile food cart services across the park.

Gaining a better understanding of Galaxy’s food and beverage capabilities has also encouraged managers to develop more creative ideas: “Being able to fully understand Galaxy for food and beverage has enabled us to grow Grab & Go offerings on little carts,” Morales says.

The Living Desert Zoo and Gardens' early results are encouraging, with increased guest demand causing lines at its seven self-service kiosks during peak days.

Sales have grown since implementation, and managers are more comfortable with the platform, introducing more creative menu items and promotions. The key opportunity is to further cut the time from order to food delivery.

​Looking ahead


“The whole vision is to eventually operate a full sit-down restaurant,” Morales says. “We’re planning to build an events center within the next five to ten years.”

That future includes table service, open tabs, bar service, and expanded hospitality offerings. While Galaxy currently excels in quick-service environments, staff sees potential for the platform to evolve with the attraction’s ambitions.

Future updates, like SMS order notifications, expanded QSR features, simplified menu management, faster inventory updates, audit logs for changes, and kiosk lockdown for easier device management, will enhance real-world functionality.

“Overall, we’re very satisfied,” says Morales of the project. “I would definitely recommend Galaxy for food and beverage. And I’d also recommend talking to other customers who are already using it before you implement. Learning from their experiences can make a huge difference.”

Today, Galaxy is a key part of the attraction’s food and beverage strategy, streamlining operations, boosting sales, enhancing member engagement, and supporting future growth.

Gateway Ticketing Systems, Inc. also recently worked with the USS Midway Museum to integrate DonationMatch and Galaxy Connect to strengthen the organisation's charitable giving programme. Since the implementation in February 2026, the museum has given 2,481 tickets, equating to $101,721, through the platform.

title: From park to place: Tim Sypko on Hong Kong Disneyland’s next chapter
summary:
When Tim Sypko describes Hong Kong Disneyland Resort as a “second home”, the phrase carries more weight than the familiar language of corporate arrival.


Sypko has spent 35 years with Disney, beginning in frontline operations and progressing through workforce management, guest experience and senior leadership. He has also spent almost seven years in Hong Kong.

Taking over as managing director is therefore less an introduction to a new place than a return to one he already understands through its daily rhythms: how guests move, how cast members perform, how weather changes behaviour, and how a destination becomes part of a city’s identity.

“There is no place in the world quite like Hong Kong Disneyland Resort," he tells us.

"As the only Disney destination surrounded by both majestic mountains and the sea, our resort offers a uniquely immersive retreat where Disney magic meets the beauty of nature.

“Stepping into this role is an exciting opportunity to build on the resort’s strong momentum and contribute to Hong Kong’s tourism growth."

His appointment comes at a defining moment. World of Frozen has established a new creative landmark for the resort. The 20th anniversary has broadened its entertainment and destination programming. New Pixar- and Marvel-themed projects are under construction.


At the same time, Hong Kong itself is repositioning its tourism offer around major events, cultural institutions, integrated resorts and closer movement across the Greater Bay Area.

For Sypko, the future of Hong Kong Disneyland is not simply about expanding the park. It is about strengthening the resort’s relationship with the wider destination and giving visitors more reasons to remain, return and connect.

​Leadership as stewardship


Sypko’s background in operations shapes how he approaches growth. Expansion is often described through new attractions, hotels, land, or shows. Yet a theme park is ultimately sustained through thousands of less visible decisions.

A well-designed environment may establish the possibility of immersion, but it is the cast member, maintenance team, performer, chef or ride operator who preserves it from one moment to the next.

“At Hong Kong Disneyland, our experiences are steeped in storytelling, and it is through operational excellence that our cast members deliver exceptional guest experience,” says Sypko.

“Every detail—from cast member interactions to the environment, attraction, food and beverage—is designed to support the narrative and sustain a sense of immersion.”

In this sense, operations function almost like stagecraft. Their purpose is not always to be noticed. They create the conditions in which the guest can believe in the world being presented.


Sypko points to Jungle River Cruise, where the skippers’ live narration and interaction make each journey personal. The sets create the setting, but human delivery gives it timing, humour and life.

This understanding also informs how the resort responds to challenges beyond the creative brief.

Over the past year, Hong Kong’s tourism sector has faced shifting travel patterns, economic uncertainty and increasingly extreme weather.

The resort has introduced stronger heat-mitigation measures and expanded products that remain comfortable and engaging under different conditions.

The Moana-themed Wayfinders’ Table, for example, combines narrative design with sheltered dining.

It is a practical intervention, but one that reflects a larger principle: guest comfort does not sit outside the story. It determines whether the story can be experienced fully.

​World of Frozen as a destination anchor


The opening of World of Frozen in November 2023, the world’s first and largest Frozen-themed land, gave Hong Kong Disneyland a distinctive international proposition.

The Frozen Ever After and Wandering Oaken’s Sliding Sleighs attractions sit within a wider Arendelle ecosystem of architecture, performance, merchandise, food and character encounters.


As a result, guests aren’t just consuming a familiar franchise; they are invited to occupy its world.

“Today’s guests are increasingly drawn to experiences that are immersive and engaging,” says Sypko. “At Disney, every experience begins with the story, the feeling we want to create and the journey we invite guests to take.”

A successful themed land is not merely a representation of a fictional place; it is an emotional structure. Its buildings, sounds, food and interactions provide different routes into the same narrative, allowing guests to develop their own relationship with it.

Hong Kong Disneyland is continuing to deepen that relationship.

A self-walking, free-roaming Olaf, developed by Walt Disney Imagineering Research & Development using next-generation robotics and reinforcement learning, introduces an element of spontaneity.


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Hong Kong Disneyland (@hkdisneyland)

Rather than waiting in a formal character-meet setting, guests may encounter Olaf as if he were moving naturally through Arendelle. The technology is sophisticated, but its purpose is simple: to reduce the distance between the imagined world and the physical one.

This reflects Sypko’s master-planned view of expansion. New elements should not operate as isolated attractions; they should strengthen the entire environment.

“We take a holistic approach,” he says. “Every new addition is designed from the outset to integrate with our existing operation and how stories are experienced.”

​From attendance to emotional value


The commercial success of a new land can be measured through attendance, spending and repeat visitation. However, Sypko returns repeatedly to a less tangible idea: emotional value.

“True success lies in the depth of connection we build with our guests and the lasting emotional value we create,” he says.

Experiences including the Castle of Magical Dreams, World of Frozen and the 20th anniversary celebrations are intended to generate more than immediate satisfaction. Their deeper value lies in the memories they hold.


A theme park is often understood as a collection of attractions. But it can also be understood as an architecture of shared time. A child’s first encounter with a character, an annual family visit or a seasonal celebration may later become part of how that person remembers a period of life.

This is where Sypko’s emphasis on repeat visitation becomes more than a commercial metric.

Returning to a park means encountering both the destination and one’s earlier self. The physical place remains recognisable, but the visitor has relatively changed.

Hong Kong Disneyland therefore measures success through guest satisfaction, affinity, advocacy and the willingness of visitors to continue the relationship. Young adults extend the resort’s stories through social media, photographs and self-created narratives.

They are not passive audiences. They participate in the construction of the resort’s meaning.

​Building an integrated resort


This emotional relationship is increasingly supported by a more integrated destination model.

For Hong Kong Disneyland, the theme park, hotels, restaurants, seasonal entertainment, retail and multi-day products are components of a single visitor journey.

Two-day tickets and combined park, hotel, dining and merchandise packages make the resort easier to navigate while encouraging longer stays. Hotel programming extends Disney storytelling beyond park operating hours, while seasonal events create reasons to return throughout the year.

This model becomes particularly important in Hong Kong, where visitors can combine Disneyland with museums, shopping, heritage districts, waterfront experiences, concerts and international sporting events within a relatively compact city.

Rather than viewing these attractions as competitors for limited time, Sypko sees the opportunity in connection.


“By working closely with government and industry players, and creating synergies with other attractions and citywide initiatives, we aim to contribute to Hong Kong’s positioning as a leading, world-class tourism hub,” he says.

Hong Kong Disneyland has already explored collaborations involving tourism destinations, major artists and entertainment platforms, including G-Dragon, BLACKPINK, World Table Tennis and esports.

These collaborations allow the resort to participate in the wider cultural calendar of the city rather than operating as a self-contained island.

The strategy acknowledges a fundamental change in tourism. Visitors increasingly assemble their own journeys from multiple experiences.

A theme park may be the central motivation for travel, but the overall value of the trip depends on how well it connects with accommodation, transport, cultural experiences, dining and other attractions.

The strongest destinations are therefore those in which different assets reinforce one another.

​Hong Kong within the regional visitor economy


Hong Kong Disneyland serves local residents, mainland visitors, Southeast Asian families and international tourists, each with different expectations and travel behaviours.

For mainland China guests, digital convenience and pre-visit engagement are key. Hong Kong Disneyland uses platforms such as its Tmall Global flagship store and major social channels to support planning, merchandise access and continued interaction.


For Southeast Asian visitors, who often travel in family or multigenerational groups, the resort focuses on multi-day products, seasonal celebrations and park-exclusive experiences that justify a longer stay.

These approaches reflect more than market segmentation. They recognise that a regional destination must be legible from different cultural and practical perspectives.

The Greater Bay Area further expands this context. As transport connections deepen between Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Macao and surrounding cities, Hong Kong Disneyland can function as part of a broader multi-destination itinerary.

This creates opportunities but also intensifies competition.

Visitors across Asia have access to an increasing number of theme parks, resorts, cultural venues and urban entertainment districts. Hong Kong Disneyland cannot rely solely on brand recognition. It must continue to distinguish itself through quality, intimacy and the specificity of its location.


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Hong Kong Disneyland (@hkdisneyland)

Its scale can be an advantage. Compared with some larger destination resorts, Hong Kong Disneyland offers a more compact and navigable experience.

Combined with Hong Kong’s urban density, transport network and cultural offer, this allows visitors to integrate Disney into a wider city break without sacrificing depth.

​Seasonality as a reason to return


Seasonal programming is another pillar of the resort’s integrated strategy.

Pixar Summer Fest demonstrates how limited-time content can activate multiple areas of the resort. The programme includes the Pixar Water Play Street Party, the new Pixar Pals Spectacular, character appearances, dining, merchandise and hotel experiences.


“Seasonal programming plays a critical role in our long-term strategy to strengthen Hong Kong Disneyland’s position as a premier destination for celebrations in the region,” says Sypko.

Summer, Halloween and Christmas each create a different emotional atmosphere. They refresh familiar environments without requiring constant physical reconstruction and allow guests to develop recurring traditions.

Seasonal events also show how IP can be used dynamically. Rather than existing permanently in a single land, Pixar stories can move through daytime entertainment, nighttime spectaculars, hotels and dining.

The resort becomes a space capable of presenting different moods and stories across the year.

​The next chapter: Pixar and Marvel


Hong Kong Disneyland’s next physical expansion is already underway.

A new Pixar entertainment experience is due to debut in 2027. It will invite guests into an immersive theatrical adventure centred on play and friendship, combining physical performance with digitally enabled environments.

A new Marvel-themed experience will follow, developed specifically for Hong Kong. It will include an attraction, immersive entertainment and retail, bringing guests into a narrative inspired by Tony Stark’s vision for a better future.


The story will bring the Avengers and their allies to Hong Kong to showcase new technologies and inventions.

For Hong Kong Disneyland, the coming Pixar and Marvel projects therefore represent more than additional capacity. They will broaden the range of experiential formats within the resort and deepen its connection with regional audiences.

​A changing entertainment landscape


The future of Hong Kong Disneyland must also be considered within Hong Kong’s expanding themed entertainment scene.

The city’s visitor economy now includes not only Hong Kong Disneyland and Ocean Park, but M+, the Hong Kong Palace Museum, Kai Tak Sports Park, large-scale concerts, immersive exhibitions, waterfront programming and IP-led retail experiences.

The boundaries between tourism, culture, sport and entertainment are becoming more indistinct.

Museums are adopting immersive storytelling. Retail developments are introducing participatory experiences. Sporting venues are becoming entertainment districts. Theme parks are functioning increasingly as cultural and hospitality resorts.


This convergence supports Sypko’s emphasis on collaboration. Hong Kong’s competitiveness will depend not only on the strength of individual institutions, but on whether they can create a coherent destination together.

A visitor rarely remembers a city through organisational boundaries. They remember sequences: an arrival, a meal, an exhibition, a performance, a hotel, a view, a moment of surprise.

Destination integration is ultimately the art of making these separate experiences feel like parts of one journey.

​From milestone to momentum


Hong Kong Disneyland’s 20th anniversary provided a moment to celebrate what the resort has become. Sypko’s task is to ensure that the anniversary does not become an endpoint.

World of Frozen has established a stronger international identity. Seasonal programming is expanding. Pixar and Marvel projects are advancing. Robotics and digital systems are creating new forms of interaction. Collaborations are positioning the resort more firmly within Hong Kong and the wider region.

Yet Sypko’s vision remains rooted in something more human than technology or scale.

The future of Hong Kong Disneyland depends on its ability to create belonging: between guests and stories, between the resort and the city, and between memorable experiences and the everyday lives visitors eventually return to.


Technology can make Olaf walk freely. New attractions can expand capacity. Hotels and collaborations can extend a stay. But the enduring value of the resort lies in whether these elements combine into something that feels personally meaningful.

For Sypko, the success of tourism is measured not only by visitor numbers, but by the lasting impression that an experience leaves. Hong Kong's mix of culture, entertainment and natural attractions provides many opportunities to create memorable visits.

At Hong Kong Disneyland, cast members play a key role in bringing Disney stories to life, helping to create shared experiences that visitors remember long after their trip.

title: Disney reports strong parks growth as AI investment accelerates
summary:
Disney has reported higher revenue and income for its theme parks segment in the three months ending 27 June, also highlighting its use of artificial intelligence (AI) to drive growth.

In its third-quarter earnings, Disney reported a 10 percent rise in revenue from $9.086 billion to $9.968bn for its theme parks and experiences. Additionally, operating income grew by 20 percent from $2.516bn to $3.017bn.

Attendance rose by 4 percent year-over-year at Disney's global attractions, with particular strength at Walt Disney World and additional capacity at Disney Cruise Line.

Disney investing to "sustain growth"

Disney's CEO Josh D'Amaro said the company is "proud of the growth that we’ve had this year, and we’re investing to sustain that growth".

“The pipeline includes major attractions at every site, including Villains Land in Orlando and the Avengers Campus expansion in Anaheim, amongst others in the US, and our previously announced cruise ship expansion,” he added.

In the third-quarter earnings, Disney said it views emerging technologies such as AI as "a significant opportunity for our company to drive returns".

The company is using AI to design, build and operate its parks and experiences, including AI-powered digital twins and simulation tools to design and test new attractions, which are being leveraged for the new Abu Dhabi park.

Disney is using AI to design, build and operate its parks and experiences, including the new Abu Dhabi park

Disney has also made its J.A.R.V.I.S. AI tool available to more than 2,000 Imagineers, and is applying AI to simplify the booking and planning experience for guests.

"Our company was founded on the convergence of creativity and breakthrough technology – and continuing that tradition is a priority for me and this leadership team," D'Amaro said.

"That’s why we’re leveraging AI to bring the most innovative tools to our storytellers.

"As I’ve said before, AI isn’t simply about efficiency – it’s about enhancing a creative process that will always be human-centered, artist-driven, and creator-led."
